newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - U.S. a bolt-hole amid EMU upheaval.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - U.S. a bolt-hole amid EMU upheaval.

text.p: Tension over monetary union in Europe will enhance the outperformance of U.S. Treasuries longer term as investors flee across the Atlantic to take cover, analysts said on Friday.

But key May payrolls data next week and the perceived inevitability of a U.S. rate rise will keep Treasuries in a stranglehold near term, making profits out of intra-day moves hard to come by, they added.
"Broadly, a big supporting factor for the U.S. will be the problems of Europe," said Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas Capital Markets here.
"Strategically, people should be buying into any weakness in the Treasury market. We're looking for the 10-year Bund spread to fall to 50 basis points in six to 12 months then to go towards flat."
"If you're not in this trade yet, get in because there's still a lot more to go."
Analysts said shorter term, the relative performance of the Treasury market next week would be partly dependent on the outcome of the French election on Sunday.

"That will be crucial," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International here. "If EMU jitters continue into next week, the overriding factor will be switches out of Europe into Treasuries," he said.
But he added it could work the other way. "If the French centre-right come through with a reasonable victory on Sunday, the safe haven flows that we've seen this week could reverse a little."
By 1113 GMT, the 10-year Treasury/Bund spread was at 90 basis points, down from 99 basis points on Tuesday.

The prospect of victory for the less fiscally austere left in France combined with a public squabble between the German government and the Bundesbank over Bonn's plans to revalue its gold, have taken their toll on European markets this week and given Treasuries a boost.

But with an onslaught of data next week, including the last payrolls number ahead of the July 2 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, Treasuries were unlikely to break out of their recent tight trading range.
Analysts were split on the likely strength of the payrolls data and the implications for U.S. interest rate expectations, and so were divided over the best part of the curve to plump for.

Paribas' McDevitt was reluctant to take a big position ahead of the figures -- "you get killed if you punt too aggressively on these numbers" -- but said if anything, the five-year sector was the place to be.
"We're looking for the curve to adopt a flattening bias, but if the figures are bad, weakness would be led by the 10-year sector, so I'd probably be in around five years," he said.
Michael Derks, cross market fixed income strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, suggested heading for the longer end of the curve.

"Up to the payrolls, I'd be inclined to play the market from the long side," he said. "I'm not convinced the numbers will increase the chances of a rate hike in July...and there's probably not enough information between these last two meetings for the Fed to tighten."
He said trying to make a directional call on the U.S. Treasury market was extremely difficult and he predicted more choppy trade with few opportunities to play intra-day moves ahead.
"The smartest money to be made is by continuing to take advantage of EMU convergence plays," he said.
"Our contention is that Bonn's gold revaluation plans will increase the probability of Italy joining in the first round of EMU."
He suggested buying Italy against Bunds and Spanish bonds, which have gone a lot further in pricing in EMU membership. -- International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
